newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk shipyard jobs may be saved, receiver says.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk shipyard jobs may be saved, receiver says.

text.p: The man handling the receivership of Poland's failed Gdansk shipyard on Friday welcomed a government plan to keep part of the company alive, saying it could result in the saving of up to 2,000 jobs.

The Solidarity trade union, meanwhile, continued a nationwide protest against the government led by ex-communists by staging rallies and marches in Warsaw and in provincial cities in the shipyard's defence.

Gdansk shipyard receiver Andrzej Wiercinski said he would study Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz's package for the yard, unveiled in parliament on Thursday, which provides for using the firm's assets to build five ships for PZM, a Polish merchant shipping company.
"I think it is a realistic project, but the difficulty lies in the details," Wiercinski told Reuters, adding he would work out ways to implement the plan by the end of April.

He said that despite the rescue scheme he would have to go on dismissing the last 3,800 workers at the shipyard, which was declared bankrupt last August with debts exceeding 415 million zlotys ($138 million).

Under the scheme, the successful Szczecin shipyard would set up a new subsidiary with the use of the Gdansk yard's assets to build the ships, for which the government would offer partial credit guarantees.
"Between 1,100 and 2,000 people could be employed under the proposal," Wiercinski said.

PZM spokesman Krzysztof Gogol said his company was planning to contract five ships worth $30 million each. "It is probable that Szczecin (shipyard) could get the contract and their construction could take place in Gdansk," he said.

But Solidarity, which leads a right-leaning electoral bloc to challenge Cimoszewicz's ex-communist party in this year's parliamentary polls, decided to go on with protests despite the prime minister's rescue package, saying the scheme left too many questions unanswered.
The union said it was also protesting against what it termed the brutality of police who used force on Wednesday to remove unionists from three ministries they had occupied.

The ex-communist party, the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), lashed out at the Solidarity over attacks this week on its offices, which it said were sponsored by the union, during street protests in Warsaw and Gdansk.
The party branded the attacks -- which involved window smashing, paint throwing and even the hurling of fire-bombs -- as assaults on democracy and freedom.
Solidarity and the ex-communists have accused each other of trying to gain political capital by stirring unrest before parliamentary elections, which a due some time around September.

A mid-March opinion poll by the public CBOS agency, published on Friday, showed Solidarity Election Action (AWS) in the lead among political parties with 24 percent support, closely followed by the SLD with 23 percent.
